text: December 5, 2014 - To accelerate the discussion, these thirty-eight languages may be conveniently grouped into ten sub-branches as follows, listed here with older names and the single-letter abbreviations used in this essay: (1) Saamic (Lapp; L); (2) Fennic (or Baltic-Finnic; F); (3) Erzya and Moksha Mordva (M); (4) Mari (Cheremis; C); (5) Permian (P; = Udmurt, Komi-Permyak, Komi, and Komi-Yazva); (6) Hungarian (H); (7) Mansi (Vogul; V); (8) Khanty (Ostyak; O); (9) South Samoyedic (Selkup and a range of extinct language varieties, most commonly identified under the names Kamass and Mator; S); (10) and North Samoyedic (Nganasan, Tundra and Forest Enets, Tundra and Forest Nenets, N). Given their current status it should be evident that eight of the ten branches of the Uralic family are threatened with extinction; this chapter aims to highlight some of the diversity that will be lost.3
